title: Bark beetle and drought tree die-off did not decrease canopy gleaners on western US bird survey routes in 1999-2025, unlike wildfire; woodpecker increases were uncertain
abstract: We tested whether tree die-off from drought and bark beetles changes breeding bird groups on western US Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes, and whether the change agrees with the wildfire result of sci:f6fee9fe (woodpeckers +11%, canopy gleaners -11%). We put USDA Forest Service aerial-survey (IDS) mortality polygons for 1997-2025 (Regions 1-6, fire, wind, flood and human causes removed) on 400 m route footprints and stop circles of 1,220 western routes, and used BBS counts and the same family-based groups and estimator as the wildfire study. The pre-registered stacked design had only 19 events and 11 control routes and gave no clear effect. With post hoc window-clean controls (42 events, mostly 2002-2004 onsets, 82 controls), canopy gleaners did not decrease (+0.028 +/- 0.123 log units, 95%); this is above the wildfire estimate (difference z = 2.0). Within routes, die-off stops gained canopy gleaners relative to unaffected stops (+0.076 +/- 0.065), while burned stops lost them. Woodpeckers increased by the same amount as after fire (+0.104 +/- 0.143) but the interval included zero; the increase was clear only in the Rocky Mountains (+0.203 +/- 0.155) and went to zero with a trend term. A continuous panel of 417 flown routes showed fewer canopy gleaners with older die-off, but route-specific trends removed this and a within-route stop panel did not show it. Future die-off predicted more woodpeckers now, which agrees with feeding on attacked trees before needles turn red. Observer, date and run quality did not change after onset; the aerial survey covered more of the route after onset. Exploratory species estimates suggest that conifer foliage gleaners decreased and broadleaf gleaners and swallows increased. No group effect met the pre-registered replication rule. Limitations: few clean events, post hoc main designs, sketch-map position error, drought confounding, negative pre-onset bins, roadside counts and family-based groups.

Canopy gleaners did not decrease after die-off.

Continuous die-off exposure per 10% of area: older die-off (OLD, 5+ years before the survey) and recent die-off (REC, last 5 years), for routes, routes with route-specific trends, and stops within routes. The route-level canopy decrease disappears with route trends and within routes.

Event-time profiles for window-clean route stacks (filled circles) and within-route stop contrasts (open squares), with the wildfire effect band. Route-level bins 3-5 years before onset are below zero, so part of the positive route estimates can be trends.
